# Wasserstein GAN
The Wasserstein GAN (WGAN) addresses the limitations of standard Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) by replacing the Jensen-Shannon divergence with the Wasserstein metric (Earth Mover's Distance). This modification ensures that the discriminator provides stable and informative gradients even when the generated data distribution and the real data distribution have disjoint supports, a common issue in high-dimensional spaces like ImageNet. In the WGAN framework, the discriminator (or critic) is constrained to have a bounded Lipschitz norm, preventing unbounded gradients that can destabilize training.
To enforce this constraint, several methods are employed, including weight clipping, spectral normalization, and gradient penalty. Spectral normalization, which scales the weight matrices of the discriminator to ensure the Lipschitz constant remains below a threshold $K$, is a prominent technique. By optimizing the objective function $\mathbb{E} *{x \sim \mu_G}[D(x)] - \mathbb{E}* {x \sim \mu_{ref}}[D(x)]$, the generator is incentivized to minimize the Wasserstein distance to the real data distribution. This approach mitigates mode collapse and allows for more robust training of GANs, particularly in complex image generation tasks.
